findings.title: Executes unverified remote script at image build time
findings.whyItBreaks: curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh downloads an unsigned, unpinned script from a third-party host and executes it with no checksum or version verification. Whoever controls that URL (or its DNS/CDN/TLS path, or the domain itself — example.com is an IANA-reserved placeholder domain) controls arbitrary code execution inside the image build, and the compromise is baked into every image layer produced from this Dockerfile. No repo artifact (docs, config, or app code) references install.sh or example.com, so the script's provenance and necessity cannot be established from the repo.

findings.title: curl|sh pipeline masks download failure, build succeeds anyway
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline's exit status is that of the last command (sh), so a curl failure (DNS/connect/TLS error, or HTTP 404 — curl without -f exits 0 on HTTP errors and pipes the error body) still yields exit 0. The RUN layer is reported successful and cached, and the resulting image silently lacks whatever install.sh was supposed to install; /app (CMD, Dockerfile:5) then runs in an environment where the dependency is missing, with no signal anywhere that the install ever failed.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault discards the error from Load and returns the zero value "". Callers cannot distinguish (a) key absent — Load returns ("", ErrMissing) at src/store.go:10 — from (b) key present with an empty stored value, and the name promises a 'default' while implementing only the zero value with no way to detect the failure. Every future caller of this exported API is forced to conflate failure with a real value and may persist, bill, or report the fallback as real. No caller can recover the error signal once this helper is used.

findings.title: Fix Run returning before goroutines finish — completion race / closed-channel panic
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, `results <- j * 2` ran synchronously: when `Run` returned, every result had been sent, so any caller could safely close `results` or proceed after the call. At head, each send happens in a detached goroutine, so `Run` returns while zero to N sends are still pending. Any existing caller that follows the base contract — e.g. `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` or `Run(...)` then reading exactly len(jobs) results — races: it may close the channel while goroutines are still sending (panic: send on closed channel) or exit before the sends deliver (silently dropped work / goroutine leak if the receiver stops consuming). The exported function's observable contract changed from 'returns when all results are delivered' to 'returns immediately' with no WaitGroup, done-channel, or documented change.

findings.title: Log's new tag parameter is silently discarded by the unchanged body
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature now accepts tags (`Log(message string, tag ...string)`), promising callers that tags accompany the log record, but the body at src/logger.go:4 still computes only `println(message)` and drops the tag entirely. Any caller writing `Log("disk full", "ERROR")` receives output identical to an untagged call; the tag signal is lost with no error or indication, so severity/context filtering downstream on the log stream silently misclassifies or drops the record. This is a public contract defect that ships now: every caller — including future ones — is forced to conflate 'tagged' with 'unlabeled'.

findings.title: Loosen `||` bypasses tenant scoping and admin requirement in canDeleteRecord
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting real values: (1) session={isAdmin:true, tenantId:'A'}, record={tenantId:'B'} → old code returned false, new code returns true: a tenant-A admin can delete tenant-B records (cross-tenant authorization bypass). (2) session={isAdmin:false, tenantId:'A'}, record={tenantId:'A', ownerId:'other'} → old code returned false, new code returns true: any non-admin user may delete ANY record in their tenant, including records they do not own (RecordRef.ownerId is never consulted). The original conjunction encoded 'admin of the record's own tenant'; the disjunction makes either factor alone sufficient, silently widening delete authorization on a public exported path even though no in-repo caller exists yet.

findings.title: clampPercent promises clamping but body returns unclamped rounded value
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public export `clampPercent` promises its result is clamped to a valid percentage, but the body is the unchanged `Math.round((done / total) * 100)` with no clamp. The sole in-repo caller relies on the promise: `progressBar` (src/progress.ts:6-8) computes `"#".repeat(pct) + "-".repeat(100 - pct)`, which assumes pct is within [0, 100]. With done=150, total=100 → pct=150 → `"-".repeat(-50)` throws RangeError: Invalid count value; with negative done it throws on the `"#"` repeat instead. Callers of the exported function and of progressBar both receive a crash (or, for external callers, an out-of-range number) whenever progress is out of bounds — exactly the input class the new name claims to neutralize.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows validation errors and returns defaults silently
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parseSettings contract changed from 'throw on invalid input' to 'return DEFAULTS', so every caller is forced to conflate parse/validation failure with legitimate default settings. The verified caller updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20) acts on the fallback: input like {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"14"} or {"fontSize":14} (missing theme) previously threw and prevented any write; now parseSettings returns {theme:"light",fontSize:14}, updateFontSize mutates fontSize, and save() persists the defaults, silently discarding the user's theme and other recoverable fields — the caller cannot detect or report the corrupt config. Malformed JSON likewise becomes a silent overwrite of the whole settings file on the next updateFontSize call.

findings.title: Restore Math.ceil so pageCount covers the trailing partial page
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount(totalItems, pageSize) returns floor(totalItems / pageSize), which undercounts whenever totalItems is not an exact multiple of pageSize. Substituting real values: pageCount(10, 3) now returns 3 instead of 4, and pageCount(5, 10) returns 0 instead of 1. The exported contract (the name `pageCount` promises the number of pages needed to hold all items) is broken: any caller that loops `for (let p = 0; p < pageCount(...); p++)` or renders `of N pages` will silently skip the last partial page — up to pageSize-1 items become unreachable/invisible (e.g., with totalItems < pageSize, zero pages are reported and all items are dropped). The positive pageSize guard on line 2 shows the function was written to be safe; the ceil→floor swap is a pure correctness regression with no compensating behavior change.

facts.meaning: The page count rounds down instead of up.
A remainder/partial final page is omitted or a small result becomes zero pages.

findings.title: Report artifacts resolved from hardcoded 'verified' ref, not the built commit
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport(branch) resolves commit = build.ref(branch) for builtFrom, but artifacts are now fetched via build.ref("verified") — a literal ref name unrelated to the branch argument. The returned BuildReport claims builtFrom=<branch commit> while artifacts are the file list of a different commit, silently misattributing artifact provenance (and if no ref named "verified" exists, ref() resolves nothing, dropping artifacts or throwing). The same inconsistency would be read by any consumer trusting builtFrom to identify the source of artifacts.

findings.title: recentEntries returns all entries; limit cap is never applied
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`; the new body returns `sorted` (the full reversed copy) for any limit > 0, contradicting the unchanged doc comment `/** Returns at most \`limit\` entries, newest first. */` and the exported signature's `limit` parameter. The added `if (limit <= 0) return []` guard does not restore the cap for positive limits. Verified consumer: `renderFeed` @src/feed.ts:9 calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and copies `page.length` entries into `new Array<string>(20)` (src/feed.ts:10-11), so with >20 entries the feed page is no longer bounded — every entry is emitted, an unbounded-output regression on the only live path.

findings.title: monthRange end drops all invoices issued on the month's final day
findings.whyItBreaks: end = Date.UTC(year, month, 0) evaluates to 00:00:00Z of the month's LAST day (e.g. monthRange(2026, 2) yields end=2026-02-28T00:00:00Z). contains() at src/lib/date-range.ts:32 is `t >= range.start && t < range.end`, so the guard at src/reports/monthly.ts:17 rejects every invoice whose issuedAt falls on the final day (2026-02-28T00:00:00Z..23:59:59.999Z). monthlyRevenue (src/reports/monthly.ts:13-19) therefore returns an invoiceCount and totalCents that omit an entire day of revenue; monthlyCsv (src/reports/export.ts:5) inherits the same understated totals into exported money reports. This is a silent financial misreport with no error signal.

facts.meaning: monthRange's end is now day 0 of the following month (the requested month's last day at midnight) instead of the first day of the next month.
Records on the last day of a month fall outside the half-open range and are omitted from monthly totals.

findings.title: Fix entry-count header to count live entries after stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: The added filter (line 20) removes stale entries from `rows`, but line 22 still passes `entries.length` to `headerLines`, so the emitted `# entry-count:` header (src/manifest.ts:15) reports the total including stale entries while fewer data rows are written. Whenever any entry has `stale: true`, the serialized manifest's declared entry count disagrees with its actual row count — any consumer that validates the header against row count, pre-allocates/sizes on it, or reads exactly `entry-count` entries sees corrupted/inconsistent output.

findings.title: execute() unconditionally throws instead of uppercasing input
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces the sole statement of the exported function `execute(input: string): string` (base: `return input.toUpperCase();`) with `throw new Error("always fails");`. Every call to `execute()` now raises instead of returning the expected string, so any consumer of this exported API fails at runtime — the function is unusable for its declared purpose, and the signature/doc still promises a `string` result (contract carrier unchanged, body implements none of it).

findings.title: Viewer rejection in isEligible removes legitimate read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, an active viewer with attempts < 5 passed isEligible and handle() returned "read-only" (src/handler.ts:25). The added line 18 makes isEligible return false for every viewer, so handle() returns "rejected" and the read-only branch at line 25 is now dead code. Viewer users who were legitimately served read-only responses are now rejected — the eligibility predicate rejects an action (read-only access) it does not govern.

findings.title: publishSnapshot serves files from 'stable' instead of the requested channel
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot(repo, channel) resolves head = repo.headCommit(channel) but then returns files: repo.filesAt(stable), where stable = repo.headCommit("stable"). For any channel whose head differs from the 'stable' branch, the returned Snapshot pairs commit=<channel head> with files=<stable tree>: the snapshot's declared commit and its content disagree, so a caller publishing or serving this snapshot ships stable-branch content labeled with the channel's commit. If the repo has no 'stable' ref at all, headCommit("stable") fails (or returns an invalid value) for every channel, breaking publish entirely. Before the change, files were repo.filesAt(head), always consistent with Snapshot.commit.

findings.title: Make build() honor the new limit parameter instead of hardcoded max_count=10
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed signature `def build(prefix, limit=10)` @ src/builder.py:1 advertises a capping parameter, but the unchanged body still uses `max_count = 10` @ src/builder.py:2 and iterates `for i in range(max_count)` @ src/builder.py:4. The parameter is never read. Any caller passing limit (e.g. `build("x", limit=3)`) silently receives 10 items — the promise (output capped at `limit`) differs from the implementation (always 10). Because `limit` affects the result a caller receives (list size), this is a public-contract defect per the TRIGGER C rule even though no in-repo caller exists yet; callers who pass the default-equivalent 10 are unaffected, masking the bug until any other value is used.

findings.title: parse_positive_int does not validate positivity or int-ness
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public symbol promises a validated positive integer, but the body is unchanged `int(value)` @src/validators.py:2: parse_positive_int(-5) returns -5 and parse_positive_int(0) returns 0. The one consumer, charge() @src/validators.py:6, multiplies the unvalidated value by 100, so negative or zero amounts are billed as -500/0 cents with no error — a caller trusting the name skips its own validation and persists a wrong charge.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code copied df and returned the copy, so the caller's DataFrame was guaranteed unchanged after apply_values. The new code writes directly into df via df.loc[...] and returns the same object, so every caller that retains, re-reads, or reuses its original DataFrame after the call now observes the overwritten 'value' column (and pandas may additionally raise SettingWithCopyWarning on views). Callers that apply mappings to multiple frames derived from one source, or that retry/log against the original data, silently operate on corrupted state — a silent data-integrity regression, not just an efficiency change.

findings.title: Move of ci.yml out of .github/workflows disables all CI checks
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub Actions only discovers workflow files in .github/workflows. After this rename the repo has zero active workflows (verified: .github/workflows/ no longer contains ci.yml at head 162bdfa), so lint and tests silently stop running on every push and PR. Meanwhile README.md:5 still promises 'CI runs lint and tests on every push', so contributors will believe unverified code is gated when nothing is checked — a supply-chain/quality regression that fails silently with no signal.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int; body accepts negative values
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public carrier `parse_positive_int` promises positive integers, but the body `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` (src/parse.rs:2) parses any i64, including negatives: `parse_positive_int("-5")` returns -5. The in-repo caller `charge` (src/parse.rs:5-8) relies on the promise and computes `n * 100`, so `charge("-5")` returns -500 — a negative charge is billed instead of the promised non-negative/zero result. The rename converts previously-honest lenient parsing into a false contract that callers (and future callers, since the fn is `pub`) will trust.

findings.title: Remove `dbg!(items)` — it moves the Vec and breaks compilation
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` expands to `match items { tmp => { eprintln!(...&tmp...); tmp } }`. `Vec<String>` is not `Copy`, so the `match` moves `items` into `tmp`; the macro's returned value is then discarded by the trailing semicolon and the Vec is dropped. The next line, `items.len()` at src/store.rs:3, uses a moved value, producing error E0382 (borrow of moved value: `items`). The crate fails to build, so every consumer of `process` is blocked. (Even if it compiled, `dbg!` leaks the entire vector to stderr in all build profiles.)

findings.title: changedPaths computed against `latest` but fromRevision pins pinnedTag
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset interface (src/changeset.ts:7-9) promises consumers 'replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision', i.e. changedPaths must be the delta computed relative to fromRevision. The diff computes changedPaths from store.resolve("latest") (line 18) while fromRevision remains store.resolve(pinnedTag) (line 17). For any pinnedTag whose revision differs from `latest`, the returned Changeset is internally inconsistent: consumers replaying changedPaths on top of fromRevision apply a delta computed against a different base — wrong files reported, edits applied against stale/incorrect content, or replay failure. Substitution: pinnedTag != latest → fromRevision=pinned_rev, changedPaths=delta(latest_rev) → replay on pinned_rev applies the wrong delta.

findings.title: Update src/query.sql to use contact_email after column rename
findings.whyItBreaks: ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN email TO contact_email makes the column 'email' no longer exist. src/query.sql:1 is 'SELECT email FROM users;' and is the repo's only consumer of this column; after the migration it raises an error (e.g. SQLite: 'no such column: email'), so every caller of this query fails on upgrade. Repo grep confirms no other reference maps or aliases the old name.

findings.title: Blocking CREATE INDEX on users table; use CONCURRENTLY
findings.whyItBreaks: Plain CREATE INDEX acquires a SHARE lock on `users`, blocking all INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on the table for the full index build. On a production `users` table this halts signups, logins, and profile updates, and any migration runner that wraps each file in a transaction cannot even run `CONCURRENTLY` as-is. This is a migration/upgrade breakage on the schema surface.

findings.title: Remove hardcoded live billing API key from source
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 7 embeds a live credential ('bk_live_9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0', prefix indicates a production billing key) directly in source. Anyone with repo read access (clones, forks, CI caches, backups) obtains production billing credentials, and the secret persists in git history forever even after deletion, so it cannot be rotated out by reverting this commit alone. The service must be able to rotate keys without a code change.

findings.title: Restoring: env-based key selection and fail-fast check removed
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed lines read BILLING_API_KEY per-deployment and threw when unset. After this change every environment (dev/staging/prod) silently authenticates to the billing API with the same committed live key, so environment-based key rotation is impossible, and a deployment that previously failed fast with 'BILLING_API_KEY is not set' now starts silently against the live billing endpoint — billing calls from lower environments can hit production with production credentials.

findings.title: Inverted isAdmin check lets non-admins purge and denies admins
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code gated the destructive delete on `user.isAdmin && project.archived` (admins may purge archived projects). The change at line 12 returns "forbidden" when `user.isAdmin` is true, so admins can no longer purge any project, and any non-admin (isAdmin=false) with an archived project now reaches `db.delete(project.id)` at line 14 and permanently deletes it — a privilege inversion on a destructive, irreversible path (data loss for legitimate use, unauthorized deletion by non-admins).

facts.meaning: The refactored guard incorrectly returns forbidden for administrators.
Non-administrators can reach the destructive project purge/delete path.

findings.title: startup() crashes with TypeError when settings file is missing
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings (app/config.py:5-7) explicitly returns None when the path does not exist. With the removed fallback, startup() now evaluates int(None["workers"]) on line 14, raising `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` on any startup where the config file is absent. Before this change, the same condition produced the documented default (workers=1, region=us-east-1) and startup succeeded. Also note the deleted default carried a second field (`region`) with no replacement default anywhere in the repo; if any deployment relied on either default, its behavior changes from working to crashing. The repo contains no caller, guard, or test that handles this: `startup` and `load_settings` are referenced only inside app/config.py itself.

findings.title: Return gateway Submit error from Charge instead of logging and returning nil
findings.whyItBreaks: Charge still has signature `error`, but the changed hunk replaces `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` with `log.Printf(...)`, so on any gw.Submit failure the function falls through to `return nil` (line 19). Every caller that checks `err != nil` to detect a failed charge now receives nil and proceeds as if the payment succeeded — orders can be fulfilled, recorded, or billed against a charge that never executed. The `invalid amount` path (line 14) still returns an error, so nil vs error is exactly the success/failure signal callers rely on; the defect ships in the contract itself regardless of in-repo callers (the package has none yet).

findings.title: Restore tenantId in cache key to prevent cross-tenant cache collision
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) at src/settings.ts:7-9 omits tenantId, so settingsFor(tenantA, name, store) caches its value under `settings:<name>` and settingsFor(tenantB, name, store) at line 13-14 hits that entry and returns tenantA's value without ever calling store.fetch(tenantId, name) (line 15). The tenantId parameter is still in the signature and is used for the store fetch, but no longer participates in cache identity — tenant B silently receives tenant A's setting (wrong-value return, cross-tenant data leak if settings are tenant-sensitive). The same change makes invalidate(name) (lines 20-22) delete the single shared entry, invalidating every tenant's cached value for that name at once, and removes tenantId from a public function's signature, an ABI break for existing callers.

findings.title: reserve() TOCTOU race: concurrent calls over-reserve after await insertion
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 15-16 read and validate `remaining` synchronously, then line 17 suspends on `await this.store.save(...)` before the in-memory decrement on line 18. Under the JS event loop, if reserve(sku) is invoked concurrently (e.g. Promise.all of two reservations) while stock is 1, each invocation executes lines 15-16 before either resumes from the await: both read remaining=1, both pass the `remaining <= 0` guard, both call save(sku, 0), and both return true. The map is decremented once total but N reservations are reported as successful — stock oversold, and the value persisted via store.save (0) contradicts the N true results returned to callers.

findings.title: Remove stale '* 1000' in retry.ts after backoff() unit change
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (capped at 30_000 ms), but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still computes sleep(backoff(a) * 1000), treating the return value as seconds. Every retry sleep is 1000x too long: attempt 0 sleeps 1_000_000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s, and the 30 s cap becomes 30_000 * 1000 = 30_000_000 ms (~8.33 hours) per retry, effectively hanging the retry path.

findings.title: Stop swallowing f.Close() error in store.Save
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code returned `f.Close()` as the function result (base store/save.go, final line of Save): a close-time failure (delayed write errors on NFS/FUSE, quota exhaustion surfacing at close) was reported to the caller of Save and the save was known to have failed. The new code replaces that with `defer f.Close()` at line 13 and `return w.Flush()` at line 20, so the Close error is unconditionally discarded. Save is an exported API whose contract is `error`; every caller of `store.Save` is now forced to conflate 'file not durably persisted (close failed)' with 'save succeeded', silently losing the write. This is a present defect in the contract itself, independent of current in-repo callers (none found; grep `Save\(` returns only the definition at store/save.go:8).

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page (off-by-one loop bound)
findings.whyItBreaks: The pre-change code iterated range(start, end) over the half-open bounds; the new code uses range(start, end - 1), so page_window returns one row fewer than page_size on every page (e.g. page_window(['a','b','c'], 0, 3) returns ['a','b']). render_page and summarize both consume page_window, so every page's last row is silently missing from the rendered output while page_count still sizes pages at full page_size — data is dropped with no error. Single-row pages (page_size=1) return empty lists entirely.

findings.title: Fix inverted TTL comparison: cache serves expired entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line `if (Date.now() - entry.storedAt > this.ttlMs)` returns the cached value only when the entry's age EXCEEDS the TTL. Any fresh entry (age <= ttlMs) falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null`, so every live cache entry is evicted and reported as a miss on first read, while entries older than the TTL — exactly the ones that must expire — are returned as hits indefinitely. The cache is inverted: zero cache hits for valid data and unbounded serving of stale data.

findings.title: pruneDone leaves consecutive done jobs and mutates caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Two defects in the changed body. (1) `jobs.forEach(...)` with `jobs.splice(index, 1)` shifts remaining elements left when an element is removed; forEach then advances past the shifted element, so any job immediately following a done job is skipped. For `[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]`, index 0 is spliced, the original index-1 job shifts to index 0, forEach moves to index 1, and the second done job is never removed — done jobs remain in the pruned result. (2) The original returned a new array via `filter`; the new code mutates and returns the caller's array, so callers holding the original reference observe it being emptied mid-iteration (in-place mutation of caller data).

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard: averageAmount([]) now returns NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`. For `rows = []`, `total` is 0 and `0 / 0` is NaN, so the exported function silently changes its empty-input contract from `0` to `NaN`. NaN is not clamped or detected anywhere: it propagates into any caller that aggregates, compares, or displays the result, corrupting downstream sums, thresholds, and serialized output without any error signal. This repo contains only src/stats.ts (verified: `rg averageAmount|busiest` returns only the declarations; no other file exists), so no in-repo guard absorbs the change — the contract change ships for every external caller.

findings.title: busiest() sorts caller's array in place — restore defensive copy
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)`. `Array.prototype.sort` sorts in place, so busiest() now reorders the caller's array as a hidden side effect of a read-only query. Callers that iterate `rows` after calling busiest() — e.g. rendering in original order, index-based pairing, or diffing against persisted order — silently observe mutated, descending-amount-ordered data. The removed `[...rows]` was an intentional defensive copy; dropping it changes observable behavior for the caller's data, which the declared contract (returns `Row | null`, no mutation promise needed for a query function) does not license.

findings.title: Fix numeric sort: default sort() compares scores as strings
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() without a comparator converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically; the removed `(a, b) => b - a` did numeric descending sort. rankScores then reverses, so the 'descending' score list is wrong whenever string order differs from numeric order (e.g. [2, 9, 100].sort() -> ['2','9','100'] -> reverse [100,9,2] is fine, but [2,9] with n=1 yields cutoff 9 -> topPlayers returns the score-9 player instead of the higher player when input is [{A:2},{B:9},{C:100}] with cutoff taken from a mis-ordered list; negative scores also invert, e.g. [-5,-1] reverses to [-5,-1] instead of [-1,-5]). The cutoff at line 15 is then wrong, topPlayers (line 16) selects and slices the wrong players, and formatBoard (line 20) displays a wrong leaderboard.

findings.title: Restore hmac.compare_digest for constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the authentication gate for incoming webhooks: handle() (app/webhook.py:14) rejects with 401 when verify() returns False. Python's == short-circuits on the first differing byte, so verification time leaks how many leading bytes of the attacker-supplied signature match the expected HMAC. This is precisely the side-channel hmac.compare_digest exists to prevent; the diff deliberately removed that protection. An attacker able to measure response timing can iteratively forge valid webhook signatures without knowing the secret. This is a security regression introduced by the changed line, not a style preference.

findings.title: Apply balances inside the transaction to keep transfer atomic
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version all three statements (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside `with db.transaction():`. The head version commits `_record_ledger` inside the transaction and then runs `_apply_balances` (app/transfer.py:24) OUTSIDE any transaction. Concrete failure modes: (1) if either UPDATE raises or the process crashes after the ledger INSERT commits, the ledger records a completed transfer but neither balance changes — money is unaccounted and the invariant 'ledger entries match balance deltas' is permanently broken; (2) the two UPDATEs in `_apply_balances` (app/transfer.py:9-16) are no longer atomic with respect to each other — if the credit UPDATE (line 13-16) fails after the debit UPDATE (line 9-12) succeeds, `cents` are debited from `from_acct` and never credited to `to_acct`: actual value loss. No error handling exists at any of these points, so any transient DB error takes these paths.

findings.title: billingDay now derives date from local timezone instead of UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed lines used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; the new line uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. billingDay is an exported public function whose output is a billing-day key, so the key now depends on the runtime's TZ environment variable: the same Date instant yields different keys on UTC vs non-UTC hosts (e.g. 2026-10-12T01:30:00Z → '2026-10-12' under TZ=UTC but '2026-10-11' under TZ=America/New_York). Consumers bucketing usage/events by billingDay would mis-attribute events near the day boundary, and sameBillingDay inherits the shift: two events on the intended billing day can compare false around midnight or a DST transition. If any day keys were already computed/persisted under UTC, a non-UTC deployment silently disagrees with historical keys on upgrade — day aggregation double-counts or drops boundary events.

findings.title: Restore tenant in memo key to prevent cross-tenant cache collision
findings.whyItBreaks: memo is module-level and keyed only by account. readProfile(tenantA, acct) caches tenantA's Profile; a later readProfile(tenantB, acct) hits memo.get(acct) at line 15 and returns tenantA's Profile (wrong tenant and displayName fields per the Profile interface) without ever calling fetchProfile(tenantB, acct). Account names are not guaranteed unique across tenants, so any multi-tenant deployment gets wrong-profile data and skips the tenant-scoped fetch entirely.

findings.title: load() silently returns "" instead of raising missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, `load` on a missing key threw `missing: ${key}`, and the caller in `loadAll` (or any external caller) could catch it and distinguish failure from a real value. Now `load(k, store)` returns "" for a missing key: (1) the empty string is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty value, so callers silently process fabricated data; (2) the only in-repo consumer, `loadAll` @ src/store.ts:12, previously propagated `missing: ${key}` via `keys.map` and now returns empty strings in its result array instead — converting a hard failure into a corrupted batch (e.g. downstream writes/billing/reporting act on "" as if it were real data). The catch is also unconditional: any unexpected error thrown inside the try is swallowed to "" too. `load` is exported (public contract): every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value, which is a present defect regardless of current caller count.

findings.title: Renamed/added required Config fields silently disable timeout and attempts
findings.whyItBreaks: timeoutMs was renamed to timeout and retries became a new required field on the exported interface. Legacy Config objects (JS callers, JSON/persisted configs, or code passing the old shape) now carry timeout=undefined: Date.now() + undefined = NaN, and Date.now() > NaN is always false (src/retry.ts:8,10), so the deadline guard is silently disabled and the loop runs full maxAttempts with no timeout — a time-bounded API becomes unbounded with no type or runtime signal. Symmetrically, a legacy Config passed to retryBackground (src/retry.ts:22) has retries=undefined, so `0 < undefined` is false and the function performs zero attempts yet returns void, indistinguishable from success.

findings.title: retryBackground duplicates retry and adds redundant retries field
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground reimplements the existing retry function verbatim except that it loops on config.retries instead of config.maxAttempts, so the shared exported Config now carries two fields (maxAttempts and retries) that both mean 'attempt budget' but are read by different entry points — a caller configuring one gets the other ignored. The semantics are also ambiguous: 'retries' conventionally means extra attempts after the first, but the loop makes it total attempts, so retries=3 silently executes 3 total calls (one fewer than a caller reading the name literally).

findings.title: Field.value typed string | number but body computes value.length, breaking on numbers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported prop contract (line 2) now promises numbers are accepted, but the body (line 6) calls `value.length`. TypeScript rejects `length` on a `string | number` union (property does not exist on type 'number'), so the package fails typecheck/build; if built untyped (e.g. JS consumers or lax config), `value.length` is `undefined` for any numeric value and the input silently renders `len=undefined`. Additionally, for the previously supported string path, the component no longer renders the caller's value in the input — it renders `len=<n>` metadata instead, changing externally visible behavior for every existing caller. `Field` is exported and public; per contract rules the promise mismatch is a defect even with no in-repo callers (grep confirms zero call sites in src/).

findings.title: Echo deploy secret into workflow log
findings.whyItBreaks: `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"` writes the value of secrets.TOKEN into the job log. GitHub's log masking can fail (e.g., short or transformed values), and any party with log read access then obtains the raw deploy credential; GitHub's own secret scanning flags this pattern. If the secret is undefined, the step silently prints an empty value instead of failing, hiding a misconfiguration.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer: git patch extraction fails on diffs over 1MB
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1024*1024 (1MB); the removed option was 64MB. runGithub uses git() to produce the full patch via `git diff mergeBase headSha` (src/adapters/github.ts:140), which routinely exceeds 1MB on real PRs. When maxBuffer is exceeded, Node kills the child and sets res.error (ENOBUFS) with res.status null, so `res.status !== 0` at line 38 throws `git diff ... failed:` with an empty/misleading stderr, the review aborts, and the PR gets a failure check-run and exitCode 1 (github.ts:182-193). Previously such PRs were handled up to a 64MB diff. The sibling helpers gh() and ghText() (lines 19, 29) still set maxBuffer: 64MB, confirming the git() value was deliberate, not leftover.

findings.title: Bundle baseSha no longer matches the base the patch was computed from
findings.whyItBreaks: The bundle's `patch` and `changedFiles` are computed against `mergeBase` (src/adapters/github.ts:140-141), but the bundle is now populated with `baseSha` (line 165). When PR_BASE_SHA is set to a non-merge-base value (e.g. the base branch tip — the exact case line 139's normalization exists for, since baseSha at line 138 can diverge from headSha), baseSha != mergeBase, so the bundle advertises a base SHA that is not the parent of its own patch. Any consumer that reads baseSha/headSha for read-only verification (git diff baseSha..headSha, git show, git log baseSha..headSha) inspects a different range than the reviewed patch and can review/misclassify the wrong changes. The previous `baseSha: mergeBase` guaranteed the promise the carrier makes.

findings.title: Restore `-s read-only` sandbox flag on codex exec spawn
findings.whyItBreaks: The original line pinned `codex exec` to the read-only sandbox (`-s read-only`). Removing it lets the spawned codex agent run in the CLI's default sandbox mode, which is writable (workspace-write) unless the user's global config overrides it — so the review agent can modify or delete files in `opts.repoPath` and gain capabilities the harness never intended. This repo's code path exists to run an LLM agent on unreviewed code; dropping the explicit sandbox pin is exactly the kind of silent security-control removal that must not merge. No compensating control exists: `spawnSync` at src/shared/codex.ts:23 passes no other sandbox/env restriction, and `CODEX_BIN` (src/shared/codex.ts:13) makes the binary itself externally controllable, so the sandbox flag is the only enforcement point in this code.

findings.title: Diff base no longer pinned to merge-base; stale PR_BASE_SHA pollutes the review
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha may come from PR_BASE_SHA (line 138), i.e. the base commit recorded when the PR was opened. The removed code computed mergeBase = git merge-base baseSha headSha and diffed mergeBase..headSha, which is exactly `base...head` (three-dot) semantics and is immune to the base branch advancing after PR creation. The new code runs `git diff baseSha HEAD` (two-dot): if the base branch gained commits after baseSha, those base commits appear in `patch` as reverse changes and their files land in `changedFiles`/`changedPaths`. Concrete wrong behavior on live paths: (1) the review bundle's patch contains changes the PR never made, so the LLM reviews (and the summary reports) the wrong diff; (2) postReview -> inlineComments (src/adapters/github.ts:63) anchors findings to files the PR did not modify (changedPaths.has(f.file) passes for unrelated base-branch files); (3) classifyFiles pre-classification runs on those unrelated paths, skewing surface labels. When PR_BASE_SHA is unset the fallback (git merge-base origin/main HEAD) already returns a fork point so the change looks safe — the supported PR_BASE_SHA path is silently broken.

findings.title: Restore function replacers in template substitution to prevent $-pattern corruption
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats the replacement argument as a pattern string when it is not a function: `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, `$n`, and `$<name>` are expanded. The base code used function replacers (`() => ...`), which insert the value verbatim; this diff removes them at three call sites. The substituted values are untrusted, arbitrary content — `JSON.stringify(bundle)` includes the full raw patch text, and `bundle.patch` is any diff (shell scripts commonly contain `$$`, code comments/strings can contain `$&`, `$1`, `$<name>`). E.g. a patch containing `$$` (shell PID) becomes `$` in the prompt, and `$&` expands to the literal `{{BUNDLE}}` match, silently mangling the JSON. The corrupted prompt is then sent to runCodex with no error signal, so the model reviews wrong/garbled input and any JSON reconstruction of findings can silently diverge from the real bundle.

findings.title: normalizeFinding no longer rejects malformed findings; it fabricates defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw 'malformed finding: ...' for any missing/invalid field (not an object, invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd) and normalizeReview(raw, strict=false) explicitly dropped such findings. The new code converts the error signal into default values: invalid severity -> 'P1', invalid category -> 'bug', missing title -> 'Untitled finding', missing file -> '', missing lineStart/lineEnd -> 0. Failure is now indistinguishable from a legitimate result: an empty or corrupt agent-output finding is kept, mislabeled as P1/'bug' on file '' line 0, and flows downstream (reported, blocked on, or persisted) as if it were real, while the underlying failure (e.g. truncated/invalid model output) is silently hidden. The signature also changed (raw: any -> Partial<Finding>, strict parameter deleted), so the exported contract itself changed semantics; per policy this is a defect present at the API contract level even with no in-repo callers (repo contains only this file and no callers were found via rg).

findings.title: Restore -R repo context for gh pr view in manual dispatch branch
findings.whyItBreaks: gh pr view now has no explicit repository: the repo context would have to come from the current working directory's git remotes or GH_REPO, but this step runs BEFORE the 'Checkout PR head' step (review.yml:42-46), so $GITHUB_WORKSPACE is empty/not a git repo on a fresh runner and gh cannot resolve the repository at all (GH_TOKEN provides auth only, not repo context). Worse, gh runs inside $(...): its non-zero exit is discarded and `echo "head="` still succeeds, so the step exits 0 with empty head/base outputs; actions/checkout@v4 with an empty `ref` (review.yml:45) silently checks out the default branch instead of the PR head, and PR_HEAD_SHA (review.yml:58) is empty — the review then runs against wrong code instead of failing. Even on a reused self-hosted workspace, resolution now depends on leftover state from a prior run rather than the workflow's declared repo.

findings.title: Restore malformed-output validation in normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw `malformed review output` for a non-object raw value, a missing/non-string summary, or findings/checked/residual_risks that were missing or non-arrays. The new code removes every propagation branch: normalizeReview(undefined | null | {} | garbage) now returns a structurally valid RawReview with summary="" and findings=[], and a review whose findings field is malformed (missing, null, or non-array) is silently normalized to zero findings instead of raising. Failure is now indistinguishable from a legitimate clean review (empty findings + empty summary), so any caller that retried, requested changes, or escalated to a human on the thrown error will instead act on the empty review as real output — in a review-pipeline this is exactly the shape that turns a crashed/garbled model response into a no-findings result. TRIGGER D: exported public path; the defect is the contract itself — every caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch mode checks out wrong code and passes empty PR SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is empty, so line 29's fallback evaluates github.ref (the branch selected at dispatch, e.g. refs/heads/main) and the review tool runs against that branch's code instead of the PR head; lines 45-46 additionally pass PR_BASE_SHA='' and PR_HEAD_SHA='' into src/cli.ts. The base version resolved head/base/base_ref via `gh pr view` from github.event.inputs.pr_number whenever EVENT_HEAD was empty, so manual dispatch with `pr_number` (explicitly advertised at lines 12-14) no longer reviews the requested PR. The same change is safe on pull_request events (head.sha is always set, and fork PRs are excluded by the unchanged if: gate at line 24), which is why this regression is easy to miss.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync to prevent ENOBUFS on large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync without maxBuffer uses Node's default of 1MB. runLocal calls git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) (src/adapters/local.ts:100) to capture the full raw patch; on any repo whose base..HEAD diff exceeds 1MB, Node kills git with ENOBUFS, res.status becomes null, and the guard at line 12 throws `git diff <sha> <sha> failed: ` with empty stderr (git writes nothing to stderr for this). The core review path is unusable on large diffs, with an error message that hides the real cause. The 64MB buffer was intentional from the file's first commit (verified via git log -p), and the unchanged gh wrapper (src/adapters/local.ts:33-37) still sets 64MB, confirming this call deliberately needed the raised cap.

findings.title: Review errors post 'neutral' check, no longer blocking required checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The error handler (TRIGGER D: failure signal downgraded, not swallowed silently — it is mapped to a benign value) changed the check-run conclusion from "failure" to "neutral" for the same error path whose summary still says 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR'. GitHub treats a neutral conclusion on a required status check as satisfying the requirement, so any review-infrastructure error (API/auth failure, model failure, malformed bundle) now reports a non-failing check and unblocks merge of an un-reviewed PR. Worse, `needs_human` verdicts already map to "neutral" (github.ts:53), so consumers of the check can no longer distinguish 'review failed to run' from 'review completed and awaits a human' — distinguishability of the error signal is destroyed at the externally visible decision point.

findings.title: Execute reviewer tool from untrusted PR head instead of trusted main checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version checked the reviewer tool from `main` (path: needlefish, trusted) and ran it against a separate `target` checkout of the PR head, so the reviewed code was data, not the executor. This diff deletes both the trusted tool checkout and the `target`/`needlefish` path separation, so `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 51) runs postinstall scripts from the PR head's package.json, and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 59) executes arbitrary TypeScript supplied by the PR itself. The `if:` guard (line 24) only excludes fork PRs — any contributor who can push a same-repo branch can run arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner with a token holding `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`, and can make the review tool approve/ignore its own malicious diff. For pull_request events GitHub also uses the workflow file from the PR head, so the PR can modify this control too. The new comment (lines 3-5) claims self-review mode requires this, but the base pattern already worked for this repo: tool from `main`, PR head reviewed as target data.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Default severity for invalid/missing input downgraded P1 -> P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding is the coercion path for raw (LLM-produced, effectively `any`) review output: normalizeReview maps every raw finding through it (src/shared/schema.ts:132). When raw.severity is absent, empty, or unparseable, the base code defaulted to "P1" (a blocking-class default); the new code defaults to "P3", the lowest class that per this pipeline's own policy is not confidence-gated ("P0/P1/P2 findings require confidence >= 0.70" — P3 is not). Any finding whose severity is missing or malformed is silently demoted to the non-gating tier, so a genuine high-severity defect emitted with a malformed severity tag passes the gate instead of being reviewed. The failure is indistinguishable at every downstream decision point: the caller receives a well-formed P3, not an error, so it cannot detect that the original signal was invalid. This is fail-open on a security-review gate — the default for unverifiable input must err toward the blocking class.

findings.title: Removed severity case/whitespace normalization demotes valid values
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code normalized severity via `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before validation, so raw agent output like "p1", "P2 ", or " p0" was canonicalized to its real class. The new code validates the raw value directly against SEVERITIES, so any valid-but-uncanonical severity fails `includes()` and is silently replaced by "P3" — a verified behavior change on the changed lines: normalizeFinding({severity:"p0"}) returned P0 before this diff and returns P3 after. Consumers of the normalized Finding (verdict computation, confidence validation) act on the demoted value with no way to distinguish it from an intentionally-low-severity finding.

findings.title: Restore removal of GitHub token env vars before spawning codex agent
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version copied process.env and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawnSync (base src/shared/codex.ts:23-30). After this change, spawnSync inherits the full parent environment, so the codex agent subprocess now receives the CI/user GitHub credentials. runCodex feeds an arbitrary prompt to an LLM agent over repo content — exactly the untrusted-input surface the scrubbing existed to defend against: the agent (or injected prompt content) can read the inherited tokens from its environment and echo or exfiltrate them into command output, tool-call logs, or the review artifact. This is a deliberate credential-isolation control (least privilege for the agent child process) being reverted, and the repo contains no other code path that scrubs these variables, so nothing compensates for the removal.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard before running PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing preventing fork PRs from reaching this job. The job runs on `self-hosted` (line 18), checks out and installs the PR head (lines 20-28: `pnpm install` executes attacker-controlled pre/postinstall scripts from the fork's package.json), then executes the fork's own code (`tsx src/cli.ts`, line 35) with the workflow's `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` token. Any external contributor can now run arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner host — reading cached credentials/secrets, persisting on the machine, and mutating other PRs — which is exactly why GitHub's hardening guidance forbids running fork code on self-hosted runners. The guard also previously prevented the review tool from running on checkouts it wasn't designed to review.

findings.title: Treat explicit 0ms grace/give-up config as invalid and silently use fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs now requires parsed > 0, so an operator who sets NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 (legitimate 'escalate to SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM' config, previously honored via setTimeout(...,0)) is silently given the 5000ms fallback at lines 3-6, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 is silently given 2000ms at lines 7-10. On a hung runner, kill escalation is delayed 5s (and the give-up resolution 2s) past the explicitly configured value, with no signal that the config was rejected — the explicit config is silently rewritten to a different value.

findings.title: reviewLarge silently skips changed files not mapped to a selected hotspot
findings.whyItBreaks: sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) truncates to 6 hotspots; the removed tail-coverage block (base review.ts, comment 'never silently skip a changed file') previously pushed any uncovered changed file into a tail hotspot that was deep-reviewed in full. With it gone, every changed file outside the top-6 hotspots receives zero deep review, and checked[] records nothing about the gap, so callers cannot detect that part of the PR was never reviewed. For a PR-review gate, silently unreviewed files on large PRs is exactly the coverage failure this tool was built to prevent.

findings.title: Deep-review residual_risks are silently dropped before the verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (swallowed failure). Previously each deep pass's res.residual_risks (which its own prompt contract says include blocks=true entries, e.g. unverifiable material concerns) were accumulated into `residuals`, handed to the critic inside candidateMerged, and reachable via pruned.residual_risks into deriveVerdict (review.ts:122). Now res.residual_risks are discarded on the spot and candidateMerged.residual_risks is hardcoded to []; the critic can no longer see any deep-pass unknown, so the final verdict can report no residual risks — and pass — even when a sub-review explicitly flagged a blocking gap. Failure signal is irrecoverably lost at the merge step.

findings.title: Critic prompt no longer receives BASE/HEAD, losing its git context
findings.whyItBreaks: Both critic invocations (reviewSmall review.ts:59-61 and reviewLarge review.ts:115-117) stopped substituting {{BASE}}/{{HEAD}}. The base code performed these substitutions at both call sites, so prompts/critic.md almost certainly contains those placeholders; the critic now receives literal '{{BASE}}'/'{{HEAD}}' text (or, if the template omits them, no SHAs at all). For reviewLarge this is worse: the critic receives only patchStat with the hint 'repo at head' and no way to run `git diff base..head`, so it must prune findings without ever inspecting the actual patch — silently degrading the false-positive-suppression gate for every large-PR review.

findings.title: formatDuration can output "60s" (e.g. "1m 60s") for durations rounding up to a minute
findings.whyItBreaks: seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000) returns 60 whenever ms % 60000 >= 59500, but minutes is floored separately, so no carry happens. Verified substitution: ms=119999 -> minutes=Math.floor(119999/60000)=1, seconds=Math.round(59999/1000)=60 -> "1m 60s"; base code produced "2m 0s". Same root cause below 60s: ms=59500 -> minutes=0, seconds=60 -> "60s" where base code printed "1m 0s". Both consumers (src/shared/render.ts:75 per-call stats, src/shared/render.ts:80 total) display this malformed duration to the user on any run whose timing lands in [x m 59.5s, (x+1) m), which is ~0.5s of every minute of wall-clock time.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 despite name and error message
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function is named parsePositiveInteger and its failure path throws '<label> requires a positive integer', but the changed guard `parsed < 0` returns 0 for input '0'. Zero is not a positive integer, so the public contract (validated positive value) is false: `parsePositiveInteger('0', ...)` resolves to 0, and callers — e.g. ones feeding the value into timeoutMs or retry counts — receive a zero value on a path that previously guaranteed >= 1. The error text also now lies: the function rejects negative input while claiming to require a positive integer, so callers cannot distinguish the intended boundary either.
